strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: recent benchmarks show AL strategy effectiveness varies across datasets, models, and cycles, and committing to a single strategy is risky. REFINE addresses this with a training-free ensemble that avoids committing to any one heuristic.

The two-stage design (progressive union-based filtering, then coverage-based selection on the refined pool) is simple, principled, and modular. The union-over-intersection rationale and the role of each design choice (R, alpha, J) are well explained, and the method is easily extensible with new strategies.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 6 classification datasets, 3 modern vision foundation models (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), 10 trials, comparisons against 8 individual SOTA strategies and 3 ensemble methods (SelectAL, TAILOR, TCM), with pairwise win-rate matrices and complete learning curves in the appendix.

Strong ablation studies that isolate each component: filtering depth R, sampling ratio alpha, batches J, filtering as a preprocessing step for each individual strategy (Fig. 5), and a controlled experiment showing the refined pool captures complementary notions of value (Margin + TypiClust, Fig. 6). The finding that filtering 'fixes' failing strategies (e.g., BAIT on DINOv3) is practically valuable.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper explicitly identifies failure cases (Dopanim with CLIP, correlated or poorly-designed ensembles) and discusses them rather than hiding them. A practical audio spectrogram use case (ESC50) demonstrates workflow-agnostic applicability.

Code availability is promised, the setting is well-specified (frozen backbones, linear head, fixed protocol from prior work), and hyperparameters are fixed across all experiments after tuning on one held-out dataset.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is largely descriptive rather than predictive. Theorem 1 is a straightforward union/probability bound; Theorem 2's exponential reduction follows directly from the definition of epsilon-uninformativeness; and Theorem 3 essentially assumes its conclusion—the assumption that higher-value instances are selected with higher probability by all strategies is exactly the property that makes filtering work, so the 'guarantee' of non-decreasing expected value adds limited insight. None of the theorems connect filtering to downstream model accuracy.

Computational overhead is significant: each AL cycle runs M strategies x J batches x R rounds, multiplying the selection cost relative to any single strategy. The paper provides an asymptotic complexity argument and notes parallelizability, but no empirical wall-clock/memory measurements are reported, making it hard for a practitioner to judge the trade-off.

Hyperparameters (R=5, J=10, alpha=0.4) were tuned on CIFAR-10 with a grid search, and the ablations on R, alpha, J use only two datasets (CIFAR-10, Snacks) with random sampling as the downstream selector; robustness of the hyperparameters across the full benchmark is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Standard errors are omitted from all learning curves and win rates are reported without significance testing; given the small margins in some plots (e.g., Dopanim), the statistical strength of some comparisons is difficult to assess.

Evaluation breadth is limited to image classification with frozen foundation models and a linear head; it is unclear how the approach behaves when the backbone is fine-tuned (where uncertainty signals and feature drift interact differently across cycles) or on other task types. The audio case study is a preprocessing demonstration only, not a full REFINE evaluation.

Some claims are overstated relative to prior work, e.g., 'the first ensemble AL method capable of effectively combining multiple AL strategies' ignores the framing of several cited baselines; also, a simple union-of-batches baseline (equivalent to a single-round ensemble) is only partially covered by the R=1 ablation and is not reported as a main-table competitor.

The final coverage selection is fixed to UHerding; while the authors note any coverage method could be used, no empirical comparison of alternative second-stage selectors on the refined pool is provided.

strengths: Extensive and well-designed empirical evaluation: 6 classification datasets, 3 foundation-model backbones, 10 trials, pairwise win-rate matrices, and complete learning curves in the appendix. The comparison against both individual strategies (BAIT, UHerding, TypiClust, etc.) and recent ensemble methods (SelectAL, TAILOR, TCM) is more thorough than typical AL papers.

The core idea of progressive filtering is simple, training-free, and clearly explained; the union-over-intersection and iterative-refinement design rationale is well argued, and the method is easy to implement and extendable with new strategies.

Ablations are informative and honest: the paper isolates progressive filtering from the final coverage stage, shows it improves even weak/failing strategies (e.g., BAIT on DINOv3), analyzes hyperparameters R, α, and J, and transparently reports a failure case (Dopanim with CLIP) plus a limitations section.
A practical use case (ESC50 audio spectrograms with an external Coreset strategy) supports the claim that progressive filtering works as a plug-in preprocessing step outside the ensemble itself.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method reduces to running M existing AL strategies J times over sub-sampled pools and taking a union, followed by an existing coverage-based selection (UHerding). The individual components are standard, and the contribution is primarily a well-engineered combination rather than a new selection principle.

The theoretical analysis is largely circular or trivial. Theorem 3's key assumption — that all strategies are more likely to select higher-value instances, where 'value' is the unknown potential to improve model performance — effectively assumes the conclusion that the pool improves. 'True value' is never defined operationally or measured empirically, so Theorems 1–3 provide little falsifiable insight beyond restating the union/survival mechanics of Algorithm 1 in probability notation.

Computational fairness is under-addressed. REFINE runs M≈8 strategies × J batches × R rounds per cycle, which can be an order of magnitude more selection cost than any individual baseline; only a brief complexity note (Sec. 4.1) and a remark about parallelism are given. A compute-matched baseline (e.g., running a single strategy on comparable budget) or wall-clock/time-to-accuracy comparisons are missing, so 'outperforms every other strategy' conflates selection quality with selection budget.

Experimental scope is narrow relative to the claims: only classification with frozen foundation-model backbones and fine-tuned linear heads. No end-to-end fine-tuning, no detection/segmentation, no class-imbalanced settings (relevant since TAILOR targets them), and no comparison of REFINE with a trivial ensemble alternative such as randomly sampling from a union of strategy batches — an ablation that would isolate the value of the iterative filtering design itself.

Hyperparameters (R=5, J=10, α=0.4) are tuned on CIFAR-10 and the ablations on pool quality (Tab. 2) use only CIFAR-10 and Snacks, the two smallest datasets, leaving robustness of these choices on Tiny ImageNet (200 classes, 100k instances) underexplored.

Several ablation trends are weak or inconsistent (e.g., in Tab. 2b and 2c, Snacks performance is non-monotonic in α and J, with α=0.2, 0.5 outperforming the chosen α=0.4 configuration in some rows), suggesting the hyperparameter story is less clean than presented and that gains may partly come from extra stochastic sampling rather than principled filtering.

strengths: The core idea—progressive filtering of the unlabeled pool via iterative unions of strategy selections, followed by coverage-based selection—is simple, training-free, and well-motivated; the union-over-intersection and iterative-refinement design rationale (Sec. 4.1) is clearly argued and empirically supported by the ablations in Sec. 5.3.

The experimental evaluation is unusually comprehensive for an AL paper: 6 classification datasets spanning 10–200 classes, 3 modern foundation-model backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), 10 trials per configuration, pairwise win-rate matrices (Figs. 2, 4), and full learning-curve sets in Appendix D. The comparison includes recent ensemble baselines (SelectAL, TCM, TAILOR), not just individual strategies.

The paper makes a genuinely useful secondary claim—that progressive filtering is a preprocessing step that improves virtually any downstream strategy—including a demonstration that it can 'fix' failing strategies (BAIT on DINOv3, Fig. 5b; Coreset on ESC50 in Appendix B). This extends practical applicability beyond the specific REFINE ensemble.

The ablations are well designed: they isolate the contribution of filtering from specific strategies (random sampling from C_R vs U_t), study the effect of R, alpha, and J on pool quality (Tab. 2), and explicitly test whether filtering captures complementary notions of value using only Margin + TypiClust (Fig. 6).

Limitations are discussed honestly, including the case where REFINE degrades when most ensemble members perform poorly (Dopanim/CLIP in Sec. 5.2) and sensitivity to correlated or poor ensemble members (Sec. 6).
The paper is clearly written, with reproducible detail (hyperparameters, training protocol, AL protocol of [16]), and code is promised for release.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. Progressive filtering is essentially an iterated union over strategy selections—a natural generalization of existing one-step filtering ideas (DropQuery, AlfaMix) and a straightforward ensemble construction. The claim that REFINE is 'the first ensemble AL method capable of effectively combining multiple AL strategies' (Appendix D) is an overclaim given prior ensemble methods (ALBL, COMB, DUAL, TAILOR, TCM).

The theoretical analysis, while correctly proven, is of limited depth. Theorem 1 and 2 follow directly from the algorithm's probabilistic structure, and Theorem 3's key assumption (selection probability monotonically related to unknown 'true value' V(x)) nearly presupposes the conclusion—'value' is never operationalized (e.g., as expected error reduction), making the result somewhat circular and hard to falsify.

Computational cost is under-quantified. Running M≈9 strategies for J=10 batches over R=5 rounds is a large multiple of any single baseline's selection cost. The complexity analysis (Sec. 4.1) is theoretical only; no wall-clock or FLOP comparison against baselines is reported, which matters for a method whose main selling point includes efficiency gains from a smaller pool.

There is a mild evaluation-fairness concern: the ensemble S is composed of exactly the individual baselines used for comparison, so REFINE effectively averages the strengths of all competitors. While ensemble baselines (SelectAL, TCM, TAILOR) partly address this, those methods are weaker in the reported setup (and the authors note SelectAL was difficult to reproduce), leaving the strongest ensemble-comparison evidence somewhat thin.

Improvement margins over the strongest baselines are modest in places (e.g., ~80% win rate vs. UHerding, and clearly visible but not large gaps on some dataset/backbone pairs in Figs. 10–11); standard errors are omitted 'for visibility,' which weakens the statistical grounding of the win-rate claims.

Hyperparameters (alpha, R, J) were selected on CIFAR-10 and fixed elsewhere—reasonable practice, but the sensitivity analysis is restricted to CIFAR-10 and Snacks, leaving generalization of the chosen settings only indirectly supported.

strengths: The core idea—progressive filtering via iterative union of strategy selections followed by coverage-based selection—is simple, training-free, and well-motivated, and is clearly differentiated from existing ensemble AL methods that learn or schedule strategy switching.

Extensive and well-designed empirical evaluation: 6 image classification datasets, 3 modern foundation-model backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), 10 trials, and a broad set of both individual strategies and recent ensemble baselines (SelectAL, TCM, TAILOR, AutoAL), with pairwise win-rate matrices and statistical significance testing (Friedman + Holm-corrected Wilcoxon).

Thorough ablations that isolate the contribution of each stage: filtering rounds R, sampling ratio α, batches J, filtering as a preprocessing step for individual strategies (Fig. 5, 9), and a targeted experiment showing the refined pool captures both uncertainty and representativeness notions (Fig. 6).

Practical considerations are addressed seriously: computational/memory analysis, parallelization and runtime measurements (Tab. 3), pool-reduction statistics (Tab. 4), batch-size sensitivity, and an audio spectrogram use case (ESC50) demonstrating that filtering can rescue an externally applied failing strategy (Coreset).

The paper is candid about limitations, including the documented failure case on Dopanim with CLIP and sensitivity to ensemble composition, and includes robustness checks for class imbalance, distribution shift, and fine-tuning of transformer blocks.
Backbone-independence and comparison against a label-informed oracle (BoSS) strengthen the credibility of the claims and honestly quantify the remaining gap.
weaknesses: The method's novelty is modest: progressive filtering is essentially iterated union-of-top-k over an ensemble plus a standard coverage selection (UHerding), both existing components; the contribution is the combination and its empirical validation rather than a new selection principle.

The theoretical analysis is largely restatement of obvious probability bounds: Theorems 1 and 2 follow directly from independence and union arguments; Theorem 3 depends on the assumption that strategies favor higher-value instances, which is close to assuming the conclusion since true value V(x) is unobservable and may not align with any strategy's heuristic.

Hyperparameters (α, R, J) are tuned on CIFAR-10, yet CIFAR-10 results are still reported alongside other datasets in several tables/figures, creating a mild advantage for the method on that dataset; robustness of the fixed hyperparameters is shown only on two datasets in Table 2.

The ensemble includes UHerding, which is also the second-stage selection strategy and a strong individual baseline; this circularity may inflate REFINE's advantage in the pairwise comparisons against UHerding (80% win rate) and partially confounds the 'ensemble vs. individual' claim.

Computational overhead is substantial (M × J strategy executions per round, sequential acquisition on the order of training time, e.g., ~10 min vs. 7.5–14.5 min training per cycle) and is only mitigated by assumed parallelization with estimated parallelizable fractions; no experiment reports real parallel wall-clock times.

Evaluation is restricted to classification with largely frozen-backbone probing; the fine-tuning experiment is relegated to the appendix with transferred hyperparameters, so performance under the harder realistic regime where acquisition signals degrade during fine-tuning is less thoroughly validated.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'first ensemble AL method capable of effectively combining multiple AL strategies' relies on specific implementation choices of the competing baselines, and the reproduction of SelectAL is dismissed based on prior difficulty rather than demonstrated here.

strengths: The empirical evaluation is unusually rigorous for the AL literature: 6 datasets, 3 foundation-model backbones, 10 seeds, pairwise win-rate matrices, and formal statistical testing (Friedman test with post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Holm correction), which directly addresses known pitfalls in AL evaluation [24, 25].

The ablation program is thorough and well-designed: progressively filtering with random sampling from the refined pool isolates the contribution of filtering from any specific strategy; the two-strategy experiment (Margin + TypiClust, Fig. 6) directly tests the claim that the refined pool captures complementary notions of value; and Tab. 4 quantifies how aggressively the pool shrinks.

The method is training-free, agnostic to the backbone, and extensible; the demonstration that progressive filtering improves any downstream strategy (Fig. 5a), including 'fixing' BAIT and the Coreset use case on ESC50, is a practically useful and well-supported finding.

Robustness checks beyond the standard setting (long-tailed imbalance, OOD MedMNIST data, fine-tuning the last two transformer blocks, batch-size variation) and runtime/parallelization analysis (Tab. 3) strengthen the evidence and reproducibility. The BoSS oracle comparison honestly reports the remaining gap to optimal selection.

The paper is clearly written, the design rationale (union over intersection, iterative refinement, sample ratio) is well motivated, and the limitations section is candid (e.g., degradation on Dopanim with CLIP).
weaknesses: The technical contribution is shallow and largely heuristic. Progressive filtering is an iterative union of top-k batches from an ensemble of existing strategies, followed by a standard coverage selection (UHerding) on the filtered pool. Neither stage involves a new selection principle; the novelty is mostly in the composition.

The theoretical analysis is weak and close to tautological. Theorem 1 and 2 are elementary probability bounds under idealized independence assumptions that do not hold for real (deterministic, correlated) strategies. Theorem 3 assumes exactly what it sets out to show: the premise V(x) > V(y) => p_m,r(x) >= p_m,r(y) for all strategies and rounds essentially defines strategies as value-monotone selectors, and 'value' V(x) is never operationalized or measurable. The theorems add little predictive insight beyond restating the design intuition.

Compute fairness is a material concern. REFINE runs M ~ 9 strategies, each drawing J batches over R rounds, per cycle; sequential acquisition time is on the same order as training (Tab. 3), and comparisons against single strategies are thus not compute-matched. A control spending equivalent compute on a single stronger strategy (or a compute-weighted comparison) is missing. Parallelization helps but assumes M concurrent processes plus favorable Amdahl estimates.

There is a circularity issue: REFINE's ensemble S includes UHerding, which is also its final selection stage, and UHerding is among the strongest baselines. The reported 80% win rate against UHerding and the acknowledged failure case (Dopanim/CLIP) suggest the gains partly stem from ensembling redundancy rather than from filtering per se.

Reported improvements are modest in many configurations. Relative learning-curve gains are often only 2-5 accuracy points on frozen-feature benchmarks, and the pairwise matrix (Fig. 2) shows substantial non-wins even against weaker strategies; the 'consistently outperforms' framing in the abstract overstates the margin.

Hyperparameters (R, alpha, J) are grid-searched on CIFAR-10 and transferred; while ablations suggest robustness, the transfer assumption is only validated on classification tasks with frozen or lightly fine-tuned features, limiting generalization claims to other AL regimes (e.g., dense prediction, large-scale pools).

strengths: The method is simple, well-motivated, and clearly presented: progressive filtering (iterative union of strategy selections) plus coverage-based final selection is intuitive, and the design rationale (union vs. intersection, iterative refinement, sampling ratio) is discussed thoughtfully (Sec. 4.1).

Extensive and carefully designed empirical evaluation: 6 datasets, 3 modern foundation-model backbones (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP), 10 trials per configuration, pairwise win-rate matrices (Figs. 2, 4), learning curves for all dataset/backbone combinations in the appendix, and statistical significance testing (Friedman + Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests in Appendix E) — this exceeds the evaluation standard of most AL papers.

Comparison against four recent ensemble AL baselines (SelectAL, TCM, TAILOR, AutoAL) with strong results, plus a BoSS oracle comparison that honestly quantifies remaining headroom rather than only claiming SOTA.

The 'filtering as preprocessing' ablations (Figs. 5, 6, 9) are a valuable contribution beyond the headline method, showing the mechanism (a) improves all individual strategies, (b) captures complementary notions of value (Margin + TypiClust experiment), and (c) can rescue failing strategies (BAIT on DINOv3; Coreset on ESC50).

Honest and thorough limitations analysis: the failure case on Dopanim+CLIP is reported in the main text, ensemble-composition sensitivity is discussed, and the aggressive pool reduction (95% discarded on CIFAR-10) is transparently quantified (Tab. 4).

Supplementary material is comprehensive: full proofs, class-imbalance and OOD robustness experiments, fine-tuning (not only frozen-feature) experiments, batch-size sensitivity, alternative second-stage designs (FIR/ER-based selection), and parallel runtime analysis showing acquisition cost can be pushed below training time.

Theoretical analysis (Thms. 1-3) with proofs and numerical examples gives probabilistic guarantees on value preservation, exponential removal of uninformative instances, and non-decreasing expected pool value; the proofs are correct as stated given the assumptions.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate. Iterative union filtering is a simple aggregation heuristic that generalizes the one-step filtering already used in DropQuery/AlfaMix; the main insight is that repeated filtering concentrates the pool, which is close to folklore. The paper's own admission that 'almost any value of alpha works well' (Sec. 5.3) suggests the mechanism is robust rather than finely tuned, which is good practice but also indicates limited sensitivity to the specific design.

The theoretical results rest on strong and largely idealized assumptions. Theorem 1/2 assume strategies have well-defined, stable selection probabilities pm,r(x) independent of pool composition, and Theorem 3's monotonicity assumption (V(x) > V(y) implies pm,r(x) >= pm,r(y) for all strategies and rounds) is acknowledged by the authors as potentially not holding in practice. The analysis does not connect the abstract 'true value' V(x) to actual model-performance improvement, so the theorems validate the proxy mechanism rather than AL performance itself.

Gains over the strongest individual baselines are not uniformly large: UHerding is a strong competitor (REFINE wins only 80% of pairwise comparisons; e.g., Tab. 2/5a show +0.7% AULC gain for UHerding from filtering), and REFINE can degrade below several strategies on Dopanim with CLIP. The claimed consistency is therefore real but the margin over the best single strategy is sometimes modest relative to the added cost of running M strategies with J batches per round per cycle.

Ensemble composition is somewhat circular: S is defined as 'all individual batch AL strategies available in our benchmark' (Sec. 4.1), so REFINE is evaluated against the same strategies that constitute it; the effect of deliberately misspecified or redundant ensembles is only explored in one appendix experiment (weak ensemble members on Dopanim).

Hyperparameters (R, J, alpha) were tuned via grid search on CIFAR-10 and fixed elsewhere; while the ablations (Tab. 2) suggest low sensitivity, the tuning protocol still uses the same dataset family that dominates the benchmark, and no results on truly held-out domains (beyond the ESC50 use case and MedMNIST subsets in the appendix) are in the main text.

The statistical significance claim of 'first ensemble AL method capable of effectively combining multiple AL strategies' (Appendix E) is stronger than the evidence strictly supports — ALBL/COMB/DUAL are excluded as single-instance methods, and AutoAL reaches 97% win rate against, so the novelty claim should be softened.

Computational overhead multiplies selection cost by M·J per round; the appendix runtime analysis is helpful, but the main text could more prominently flag that REFINE is substantially more expensive than a single strategy in the sequential case (e.g., ~10 min acquisition vs. ~8 min training at cycle 10 on CIFAR-100).
